alt: A grid of six finished wallpapers, one from each fractal family.
caption: One finished wallpaper per family, and nothing else about them is hand-made: each was found by a walk, drawn in one of the rendering modes, colored from a chosen palette, and kept by a judge.

alt: The four stages as a diagram: search feeds render, render feeds color, color feeds select.
caption: The pipeline end to end. Search proposes locations, render draws them at quality, color dresses them, and select keeps the few worth keeping — the four stages the rest of this site takes one at a time.

alt: Animated: three starting points advancing in step across the plane — one escaping fast, one bounded, one lingering near the boundary — with a |z|-versus-step chart alongside.
caption: Three orbits under the same rule, stepping together. One is past |z| = 2 within a few steps and gone for good, one stays bounded forever, and one hangs near the boundary for dozens of steps before it commits. The step where a track crosses the line on the chart is that orbit's escape time — the whole of what the picture is painted from.

alt: Nine successive zooms into one point on the Mandelbrot boundary, each frame the marked box of the frame before it.
caption: One point on the boundary, magnified in stages, each frame drawn from the marked box of the one before. Nothing simplifies on the way down: spirals, filament tangles and miniature copies of the whole set keep arriving. The strip ends because the page does, not because the detail ran out.

alt: The Mandelbrot set as an atlas: four c values marked on it, each with the Julia set it produces below — a solid blob from deep inside, disconnected dust from outside, a filigree from the boundary.
caption: The Mandelbrot set read as an atlas of Julia sets. A c from deep inside gives a solid, rounded blob; a c from outside shatters into dust; a c from the boundary unfurls its neighborhood's spirals and filaments across the whole frame. The blob-versus-dust split is not a matter of degree — a Julia set is connected exactly when its c lies in the Mandelbrot set.

alt: The degree-3, degree-4 and degree-5 multibrot sets beside the classic degree-2 set, with one zoom each.
caption: Raising the power in z → z^d + c, with one zoom under each set. Every degree adds a rotational symmetry the classic set doesn't have — one fold fewer than the degree — and each carries its own Julia sets, made exactly the same way as before.

alt: Five sets at fractional degrees — d = 2.1, 2.5, 2.9, 3.5 and 4.5 — each whole in its own frame, with a close-up of the branch-cut seam at d = 3.5.
caption: Five degrees between the whole ones, each framed by the rule that gives the other families their home views. A whole degree carries its lobes in even rotation, one fewer than the degree; a fractional one is caught mid-turn between two of those arrangements, with the next lobe part-grown. Where that lobe happens to sit decides how much the branch cut shows: at 2.9 the negative real axis runs through the gap between two lobes and the render is clean, while at 3.5 the arriving lobe sits astride the axis and the halo flares where escape times jump across the cut. The close-up is that edge at eight times the frame — rays ending mid-stroke along a straight line no dynamics put there.

alt: The classic Ushiki phoenix render beside several finds from elsewhere in the (c, p) plane.
caption: The celebrated Ushiki constants beside finds from elsewhere in the (c, p) plane. Each orbit is steered by where it just was, and the feathery plumes are what that produces — structure none of the memoryless families draw.

alt: Six panels, one per family, each showing the whole set inside its own frame.
caption: Every family at its home view — the frame it draws when no viewport is given. Five of the six are derived by measuring the set and giving it a 16:9 frame with a tenth of the deciding axis to spare; a Julia set's extent depends on its constant, so it keeps the whole-plane view by exception.

alt: The same Mandelbrot view twice: smooth on the left, banded into flat contours on the right.
caption: One location, one palette, one iteration cap, two rendering modes. The discrete field is exactly the floor of the smooth one, so the difference is visible only where a frame holds few escape values — here, a cap of 50. At production caps the two are the same picture.

alt: A Phoenix set framed two ways: cropped at both lobes on the left, wholly contained on the right.
caption: Where a walk starts decides what it can find. On the left the root frame is the whole-plane default and holds 66% of the set's height; on the right it is the family's own home view, and both lobes are territory the walk can descend into.

alt: The whole Mandelbrot set drawn in two different palettes, with one boxed cutout shown below in the same two.
caption: One escape field, four pictures. The top row is the whole set in two palettes; the bottom row is the boxed cutout in the same two. Nothing about the fractal changed between the columns — the palette is a decision made after the location, and this page is about the numbers that sit under all four.

alt: One Mandelbrot location at a cap of 50, twice: terraced into flat bands on the left, continuously shaded on the right.
caption: The integer escape count beside the smooth count of the next section, at one location, one palette and one cap. Every pixel that escaped on the same step takes the same color, so the field terraces into flat contours. The cap here is a deliberately low 50: at the caps a real render uses, the terraces are finer than a pixel and the left-hand picture is the right-hand one.

alt: A finished multibrot wallpaper beside the same frame's escape field drawn as grayscale.
caption: A finished wallpaper and the field underneath it: the same numbers, once through the picture's own palette and once as plain lightness over the same working range. All of the structure is the field's. What the palette decides is which part of the field's range you get to see — which is the last section on this page. A degree-4 multibrot at a location I scored 4 of 4, colored the way I scored 4 of 4.

alt: One deep Mandelbrot location at a cap of 300 beside the same location at the automatic cap of 32,474.
caption: One location, one palette, two caps. At 300 every orbit that would have escaped in the low thousands is declared interior instead, and the flat region swells across the middle of the frame and swallows the spiral the picture exists to show. At 32,474 — what the depth policy chooses for a frame this wide — the same spiral resolves into filaments.

alt: A filament-rich Julia crop at one sample per pixel beside sixteen, both enlarged so that single pixels are visible.
caption: One crop at one sample per pixel and at the production setting of 4 × 4 = 16, both enlarged to twice size so single pixels are visible. A filament thinner than a pixel is a coin flip at one sample: the arms break into speckle and the spiral's dotted beads come apart. Nothing later in the pipeline can put back what the sampling missed.

alt: One Julia location under a cyclic ice palette at one, two, three and four sweeps of the gradient.
caption: One location and one cyclic palette, swept across the frame's range k times. At k = 1 the gradient is spent once over a range most of the frame does not occupy, and wide areas come out nearly flat; each further sweep spends it again and pulls more of the structure apart. Repetition is the classic escape from a squeezed range, and it is why so many older Mandelbrot renders are striped with rings.

alt: One Mandelbrot location with the palette spread linearly across the frame's whole range, beside the same field leveled against its own distribution.
caption: The same field twice. On the left the palette is spread linearly from the frame's lowest value to its highest, 11 to 8,504. Ninety-nine per cent of the frame lies between 11 and 64, so almost the whole picture is drawn from the first 0.6% of the gradient and the rest of the palette is spent on a handful of samples along the boundary. On the right the working range is measured from the distribution instead, and the picture was there the whole time.
